body.tipQ: Show only people whose username contains this text, in any case.
body.tipProtocol: Show only people who have signed in through this protocol at least once. The list is every protocol anyone listed here has signed in through.
body.tipFactor: Show only people in this second-factor state. "enrolment this process cannot read" is an authenticator app enrolled under a key this process cannot open. A person no credential store answers for matches only "any state".
body.tipKind: Show service accounts only, or everybody except them.
body.tipPer: How many people to show on each page.
body.tipFilter: Apply the filters to the left.
body.tipCreate: The username of the person to create. You choose their attributes and how they first sign in on the next page.
body.serviceAccountTitle: A service account: a person entry used by a program, governed by the service-account policy
body.everybody: Everybody this realm knows about, from two places and the Known from column says which. SEEN is every userid this service has been given as part of an interaction that succeeded — the name typed at either sign-in screen, the one on a password grant, the subject of a WS-Security UsernameToken, the client principal in a Kerberos AS-REQ or an accepted AP-REQ, and the subject of an exchanged token; a request that was REFUSED records nothing. DIRECTORY is an entry under ou=users, however it got there. Most people are both. Click a name for its sessions, everything issued to it, and the second factors it holds.
body.noDirectory: No directory is loaded in this process, so this is the SEEN half alone and the second-factor columns say unknown rather than none. Those are different answers and the second one is the dangerous one to guess.
body.capped: This realm holds {scanned} people and only the first {limit} were read for the credential columns. Reading a credential per person happens on the one thread that answers every socket this service holds, so the scan stops rather than stalling the service.
body.unreadable: {count} authenticator enrolment(s) cannot be read by this process — almost always a shared secret sealed under a key-encryption key that has since been rotated. Those people are REFUSED at the code step rather than let through on one factor, so they cannot sign in at all until the enrolment is cleared on their own row and set up again.
body.spiffeBefore: An identity this trust domain has only ISSUED a certificate to is here with never in the Authenticated column — it counts under “seen only as a subject”. Being issued a credential is not presenting one, and an agent re-mints every half-hour, so counting issuances would turn one workload into hundreds of sign-ins. It also gets a directory entry under ou=users carrying the certificate it currently holds — see
body.oneRow: One row is one local name, across every protocol. The same person arrives here as alice at the login screen, her urn:uuid: subject in every token and alice@STS.MOCK as a Kerberos principal, and showing three rows for that would be a worse answer than one — the premise of this service is that the name you type is who you are in every protocol at once. What it costs: two different people called alice in two Kerberos realms are one row here. The Realms column is what makes that visible. Case is never collapsed, because nothing in this service treats Alice and alice as one.
body.tipGo: Go to New user with this name filled in. Nothing is created until you press Create there.
body.takesYouRest: , carrying whatever name you type here, and creates nobody by itself. There you fill in as few or as many of the {count} attributes a person in this directory can carry as you like — only the username is required, and a box left empty records no value — and choose how they first get in: a password you type, one generated and shown once, a single-use activation link shown once, or nothing at all. There is a button there that fills the form in with the invented person this service would have made up, which is what this button used to do without asking.
body.putsAnEntry: Puts an entry in the embedded LDAP directory at uid=<name>,{container}. One entry per person: a name that is already here is refused, whichever protocol brought them and whatever attribute their entry is named by — the same refusal an ldapadd, a SCIM create and POST /admin-api/users/create get, because all of them call one function. The new user will not appear in the table below until they authenticate somewhere: that is who this service has SEEN, and this is what the directory HOLDS.
body.nobodyMatches: Nobody matches. Nothing has authenticated here yet unless a filter above is hiding it.
body.matched: {matched} {one, select, yes {identity} other {identities}} match; {known} known in total, most recently active first. An identity marked never under Authenticated has been issued something without ever presenting a credential here: an exchanged token from another issuer, a WS-Trust OnBehalfOf, or a Kerberos S4U request that a service made in their name. Listing them is the point — a users page that showed only the sign-ins would deny the existence of subjects the tokens page is showing at the same moment.
body.inMemory: All of it is in memory and dies with the process, and the registry holds the most recent {keeps} identities.
credentialCell.nothingTitle: No password and no primary security key, so nobody can sign in as this person. A second factor is never a way in by itself. An activation link on their own row is how they come to hold one.
secondFactorCell.unreadableTitle: This process cannot read the enrolment: {why}. Their codes cannot be checked, so they are REFUSED rather than let through on one factor. Clear it and let them enrol again.
sourceCell.bothTitle: This service has seen this identity AND the directory holds an entry for it. That is the ordinary state.
sourceCell.directoryTitle: An entry under ou=users that this service's own registry does not hold. The registry keeps the most recent {keeps} identities and the directory is not capped, so a realm that has been bulk loaded has many of these.
sourceCell.seenTitle: This service has seen this identity and there is no directory entry for it — a client, an LDAP bind DN, or a subject something was issued for with nobody present. Their row says which.
newUserBody.noDirBefore: There is no embedded LDAP directory loaded in this process, so there is no ou=users container to put a person in and this form is not drawn. That is a build of this service without ldap/ldap_server.js rather than a fault — every other page is unaffected, and
newUserBody.noDirAfter: still reports what this service has SEEN, which does not come from the directory.
newUserBody.lands: The entry lands in this realm's directory, at uid=<name>,{container}. The console shows one trust realm at a time and this form writes the one it is showing — {realm} — because the realm is taken from the path this request arrived on. People are NOT shared between realms: an ldapsearch with that base DN sees exactly what this creates, and another realm has never heard of them.
newUserBody.notSecondStore: This is not a second store. The form posts action=create to this page, which calls the same function POST /admin-api/users/create, a SCIM create and an ldapadd under ou=users all reach — so what a username may be, and the refusal of one that is already here, mean the same thing at every door. One entry per person is the rule it keeps, whichever protocol brought them and whatever attribute their entry happens to be named by.
newUserBody.emptyBefore: An empty box records NO VALUE. It does not fall back to an invented one. That is the difference between this page and the single Create box that used to be on
newUserBody.emptyMiddle: : that button invented a whole person — a name, an email address, a date of birth, a street, a nationality — behind whatever username was typed. Here nothing is made up unless you press the button that makes it up. What that costs is that an issued credential asserting birthdate for somebody with no schacDateOfBirth falls back to the invented value at ISSUANCE time (vc_claims.js does that so a credential is never empty), so the credential and the directory will disagree until somebody fills the attribute in.
newUserBody.emptyAfter: is where that fallback is described.
newUserBody.usernameHint: the name they sign in as
newUserBody.onlyRequired: The only required field. It is the string they will type at a sign-in screen, the sub of every token issued for them, the uid on the entry and the name of the entry itself. It may not be a DN, a did:, a SPIFFE identity or carry a character RFC 4514 reserves in a DN (, = + < > # ; " \) — those name entries that reach this directory by being PRESENTED rather than created, and the refusal names which one you sent. Case is never collapsed: nothing in this service treats Alice and alice as one person.
newUserBody.passwordReadOnly: Read ONLY when A password I type is chosen above; ignored otherwise, so a value left in these boxes cannot become a credential nobody meant to set. The two must match.
newUserBody.notChecked: , and this realm is in development mode, where no password is checked at any door — so the rule is not applied to what you type here. A generated password meets it in both modes.
newUserBody.passwordRefused: If the password is refused the person is still created, with no credential, and the page says why.
newUserBody.saLabel: Service account — a person entry used by a program
newUserBody.saBefore: Ticked, the person is governed by this realm's
newUserBody.saAfter: : by default no browser sign-in, the second factor NOT exempt, an owner required, and no rotation. The owner and the destination are checked BEFORE the person is created, so a refusal creates nobody.
newUserBody.gridBefore: Every attribute here is one a person in this directory can carry, and an attribute in the
newUserBody.gridAfter: catalogue is the value an issued credential asserts — its tooltip says which claim. Fill in as few or as many as you like. A list takes one box per value, with + to add one and the bin to delete one; an empty box records nothing.
newUserBody.uidNote: uid is not on this list and that is not an omission. It is the username, asked for once at the top; a second box for it would let one form create uid=alice whose uid says bob.
newUserBody.advancedView: Advanced view: every attribute a person here can carry.
newUserBody.simpleView: Simplified view: the names and contact details most people need.
newUserBody.switchTip: Draw the other view of this form. Nobody is created, and everything typed so far is kept.
newUserBody.fillNote: Fill with example data puts the invented person for the username you typed into the boxes you have left EMPTY, and touches nothing you have already filled in. It creates nobody — you land back on this form with the values in it, to edit or clear before pressing Create. It is the same invented person this service would have made up on its own, seeded from the username, so it shows you what you would have got rather than a second fiction. Type the username first: change it afterwards and the example person is somebody else. description stays empty because this service writes that one itself.
newUserBody.productBefore: There is no Fill with example data button because this service is in PRODUCT mode (global.mode=product). Inventing a person's date of birth, address and nationality is a development convenience; on a service running as a product it would put fictions into a directory somebody else reads as fact, and there would be nothing on the entry afterwards to say which values were made up. Type what you know and leave the rest empty. global.mode is on
newUserBody.productAfter: , with the rest of the settings that belong to no one protocol.
newUserBody.persistBefore: Nothing about this create is persisted unless this service is persisting the directory. A person here IS a directory entry, so they survive a restart exactly when it does — see
newUserBody.persistAfter: , which is off by default. That is a property of the whole service rather than of this page.
newUserBody.persistYes: This process is running with persistence.mode={mode}, so this entry WILL survive.
newUserBody.persistNo: This process is not persisting anything, so it will not.
newUserBody.notOnUsersBefore: A person created here is not on the Users table until they authenticate. That table is who this service has SEEN; this writes what the directory HOLDS, and the two are different questions on purpose. They are counted under “seen only as a subject” the moment they exist, and
newUserBody.populateBefore: Leaving a field empty is not a promise it stays empty. The Populate button on
newUserBody.populateAfter: — and the sweep that runs when a trust realm is created — fills every MISSING selected attribute on every person under ou=users, and it does not know which of them were typed by hand. That is the right behaviour for the sweep, whose whole job is that the directory and an issued credential agree; it means “no value recorded” is a statement about this create rather than a permanent property of the entry.
detail.overviewBefore: Everything below is about the identity {name}, which is
detail.oneRow: one row of the users list
detail.presented: . They have presented a credential to this service {count} time(s).
detail.neverAuthenticated: . They have never authenticated here. This identity is known only because something was issued naming them as its subject — an exchanged token from another issuer, a WS-Trust OnBehalfOf, or a Kerberos S4U request made by a service. Nothing about this row says the person was ever present.
detail.isClient: This is a client, not a person: it appears here because client_credentials produces tokens with a subject and no human behind them.
detail.pictureNote: Everything issued in their name, drawn. Every credential as a line to the application holding it, labelled with the exact OAuth 2.0 grant or OpenID Connect flow that produced it; their sign-ins as lines into this service; and any delegation naming them in the same diagram. Tokens are revoked HERE — that page draws and changes nothing.
detail.namesHeading: Names this identity has been seen under
detail.namesNote: One person reaches this service under several spellings and they are the same row here — see the note at the top of the users list for what that costs.
detail.blocksNote: The session BLOCKS below start at {blocks} rather than {per}, because each of them is itself a table; setting a size here applies to those too.
detail.sessionsHeading: Sessions, and what was issued on each
detail.sessionsNote: A sign-on session is a browser holding the sts_session cookie, shared between the OAuth 2.0 / OIDC login screen and WS-Federation. A token is placed under a session because the issuance said so — no token this service issues carries a session identifier, and OIDC's sid claim is for front-channel logout, so inventing one to make this page easier would change what every client receives. The link is recorded out of band at issuance instead, and it survives a refresh: a refreshed token is looked up by the refresh token's jti and lands under the same session.
detail.noSession: This user holds no sign-on session. That is the normal state for every identity that never used a browser here — a password grant, a Kerberos client, a WS-Trust requester — and for anyone whose session has expired and been swept.
detail.endedHeading: Issued on a session that has since ended
detail.endedNote: These name a session this service no longer holds. It is not an error and it is the ordinary end state: the session expired or was signed out, and the tokens it produced outlived it — which is exactly the position a client is in when its access token still verifies and the browser would be asked to sign in again.
detail.sessionlessHeading: Issued with no browser session at all
detail.sessionlessNote: The grants that never involve a browser: password, client_credentials, OID4VCI's pre-authorized code, and token exchange. The Grant column says which. An empty Grant means the token was minted somewhere that states nothing about how — WS-Trust's JWT and the credential issuer both sign directly.
detail.artifactsNote: None of these can be revoked here and the console does not pretend otherwise: nothing consults this service about a SAML assertion, a Kerberos ticket or a credential, so a button would change a number on this page and nothing at all out there. The only distinction is whether the validity window has closed.
detail.signOutBefore: Everything, in every protocol. This is the same act
detail.signOutAfter: performs, through the same function: it ends every browser sign-on session, notifies every OpenID Connect relying party, WS-Federation realm and SAML 2.0 service provider they signed into (an OpenID Connect relying party with a backchannel_logout_uri is POSTed a Logout Token by this service), invalidates their authorization codes and OID4VCI pre-authorized codes, closes their bound LDAP connections, stamps the Kerberos sign-out instant on their principal, and revokes their tokens. In that order — the notifications are built off the session, so ending it first would leave every federated partner believing they were still signed in.
detail.cannotDo: Two things it cannot do, and neither is a gap in this button. A front-channel notification is an iframe loaded in the signed-out person's OWN browser, and this console is not that browser — so what happens here is that the relying party is forgotten and the notification is reported rather than sent; /logout is where those actually load (the back-channel Logout Token is not one of these: it is sent). And nothing recalls a SAML assertion, a Kerberos service ticket or an SVID: each is valid because somebody else can verify it without asking this service, so the only thing that ends one is its own expiry. The Kerberos sign-out instant is the nearest thing that exists, and it refuses a TGS-REQ presenting an older ticket rather than recalling the tickets already issued.
detail.signOutTip: End every session they hold and revoke their tokens: a global logout. Back-channel Logout Tokens are sent; front-channel notifications need their own browser and are not.
detail.revokeHeading: Revoke this person's tokens, and nothing else
detail.revokeNote: The narrower act, and the one this section used to be the whole of. Every access token, ID Token and refresh token held for this identity under any of its spellings, revoked through the same set /oauth2/revoke writes to. It does not sign them out — their browser session survives, so the next authorization request mints a fresh set and this will look as though it did nothing. That is the honest behaviour of a revocation and the reason the button above exists; use this one when you want the credentials out of circulation and the session left alone. Assertions and tickets are untouched either way, for the reason above.
detail.revokeTip: Revoke every access, ID and refresh token held for them. Their browser session is left alone, so their next request is issued new ones.
sessionBlock.nothingIssued: Nothing has been issued on this session yet. A browser can hold a sign-on session and have been given no token at all — it is what the authorization endpoint reads before it issues anything.
userTokenTable.notRevocable: Only access tokens, ID Tokens and refresh tokens can be revoked — the others are replies rather than credentials, or carry no jti to act on.
userArtifactTable.noIdTitle: A Kerberos ticket has no identifier to quote: it is named by the client and service it is for.
userArtifactTable.none: Nothing that is not a JWT has been issued to this user.
authenticationTable.noAddressTitle: No client address: recorded before authentication events carried one, or not sent over a socket.
authenticationTable.none: No authentication was recorded for this identity. See above: they are known here only as the subject of something that was issued.
authenticationTable.forgotten: The most recent {max} of {total} authentication(s); the rest have been forgotten. The counts above them are of all of them and are not capped.
riskBadge.notAssessed: This person has not been assessed: nobody has signed in as them since risk scoring began, or it is off.
ldapObjectSection.heading: This user in the LDAP directory
ldapObjectSection.noDirectory: No LDAP directory is loaded in this process, so there is no entry to show. That is a build of this service without ldap_server.js and not a failure — every other section of this page is unaffected.
ldapObjectSection.alsoNamedRest: . Those were written through the protocol rather than seeded by an authentication — this directory has no schema and does not require a uid to be unique, so they are shown rather than merged.
ldapObjectSection.autoCreateOff: An entry per authenticated user is switched OFF in this process (LDAP_AUTOCREATE_USERS), so nothing here seeds one.
ldapObjectSection.isClient: This identity is a client, not a person. client_credentials produces tokens with a subject and nobody behind them, and a directory of people is the wrong place for it, so the directory declines to invent one.
ldapObjectSection.neverAuthenticated: This identity has never authenticated here. The entry is seeded at the moment a credential is ACCEPTED, and this one is known only as the subject of something that was issued — so there was no such moment.
ldapObjectSection.nothingSeeded: Nothing was seeded for this identity.
ldapObjectSection.ldapBind: Everything this identity has done here is an LDAP bind, which presents a DN rather than a user name. Seeding uid=<a whole DN> under {usersDn} would put a second, malformed object beside the one the DN already names.
ldapObjectSection.full: The directory holds its maximum of {max} entries, so it stopped creating them. The authentication itself was unaffected — a full directory must never fail one.
ldapObjectSection.gone: It was there and is not now: an entry can be deleted or modifyDN’d through the protocol like any other, and nothing puts it back until this name authenticates again.
ldapObjectSection.entryNote: The entry the embedded directory holds for this person — the object itself and not a copy of it, so an LDAP client bound to ldap://<host>:{port} reading {dn} sees exactly this. It appeared the first time they authenticated through any protocol here, and it carries no password: every bind to this directory succeeds anyway, whatever DN and whatever password, so nothing in this object is a credential.
ldapObjectSection.subject: Subject (sub): {subject}
ldapObjectSection.subjectNote: urn:uuid: and this entry's entryUUID, which it keeps through a rename. A person deleted and created again under the same name is a different subject.
ldapObjectSection.timestamps: The two timestamps are generalized time (YYYYMMDDHHMMSSZ), which is what a directory shows — not the ISO 8601 strings the rest of this console uses. The difference is only punctuation and it is kept because a debugger that showed one where the protocol carries the other would be showing the wrong thing.
ldapObjectSection.attributesNote: Every attribute the entry has, operational ones included. This directory is schemaless: no objectClass is enforced and no value is checked against a syntax, so an attribute a real directory would refuse is here because something wrote it. The description values are this service's own note of which protocols this person has authenticated through — one line per protocol, added the first time each is seen.
idaTips.framework: The trust framework the verification was done under (verification.trust_framework), from oauth2.idaTrustFrameworks.
idaTips.level: The assurance level reached within that framework (verification.assurance_level). Optional.
idaTips.time: When the verification was done (verification.time), as an ISO 8601 date and time. Empty records now.
idaTips.evidence: The kind of evidence the identity was verified with. Only the fields of the kind chosen below are recorded; none records the verification with no evidence.
idaTips.check: How the evidence was checked (check_details check_method), from the specification's predefined values. None records no check.
idaTips.issuer: The authority that issued the document (document_details.issuer.name).
idaTips.country: The issuing country as an ISO 3166-1 code (document_details.issuer.country_code).
idaTips.issued: The date the document was issued, YYYY-MM-DD.
idaTips.expires: The date the document expires, YYYY-MM-DD.
idaTips.recordType: The kind of electronic record (record.type), for example a bank account.
idaTips.recordSource: Who holds the record (record.source.name), for example the bank.
idaTips.vouchType: The kind of attestation the voucher gave (attestation.type).
idaTips.created: When the signature was made (created_at), as an ISO 8601 date and time.
mfaSection.heading: Second factors, and what this person can sign in with
mfaSection.noStore: No credential store is installed in this process, so nothing here can say what this person holds. That is a build of this service without ldap_server.js and not a failure — every other section of this page is unaffected.
mfaSection.passwordSet: — a scrypt hash on their own entry. It cannot be read back and this console cannot show it; the form below replaces it.
mfaSection.primaryKeyNote: — signs them in on its own, passwordless. The session then records amr ["hwk"] and acr "1".
mfaSection.cannotSignIn: — no password and no primary key. A second factor is never a way in by itself, so nothing below changes this answer. An activation link is how they come to hold a credential.
mfaSection.asksFor: — the sign-in screen asks for {factor, select, webauthn {the SECURITY KEY} webauthnOrTotp {the SECURITY KEY, with the authenticator app offered as the alternative for somebody at a machine the key is not plugged into} totp {a CODE from their authenticator app} emailLink {an EMAILED SIGN-IN LINK, the one second factor they hold} other {an EMAILED CODE, the one second factor they hold}}. A password alone will not sign them in.
mfaSection.notDemanded: — nothing here is configured as a second factor, so a password alone signs them in.
mfaSection.totpSelf: They set one up themselves at /portal/mfa, or while spending an activation link. There is deliberately no way to enrol one from here: enrolling means being shown a shared secret, and an administrative door that handed one out would mint a working second factor for any account — which is not a second factor at all.
mfaSection.totpOffBefore: Authenticator apps are switched off in this realm (the authentication policy on
mfaSection.totpOffAfter: ), so nobody new can enrol one.
mfaSection.totpUnreadable: An enrolment exists and this process cannot read it — {why}. Almost always a shared secret sealed under a key-encryption key that has since been rotated. They are REFUSED at the code step rather than let through on one factor, so they cannot sign in at all until this is cleared and set up again.
mfaSection.codeParams: {digits} digits, HMAC-{algorithm}, a new one every {period} seconds. These are the parameters the QR code told the app and are what verification uses — changing
mfaSection.codeParamsAfter: affects NEW enrolments only, because this service cannot reach into somebody's phone.
mfaSection.totpDiffers: This enrolment differs from the current settings ({digits} digits, HMAC-{algorithm}, every {period}s), which is correct and is what that sentence means.
mfaSection.skewNote: {window} step(s) either side. This one is live for everybody — how much a deployment forgives a drifting clock is a policy rather than something the app was told.
mfaSection.sealedBefore: under this service's key-encryption key, so
mfaSection.inTheClear: stored as base32, in the clear — development mode, where the key-encryption key is generated per run and sealing would mean an authenticator that silently stopped working at the next restart. Verifying a code means COMPUTING it, so unlike a password the secret cannot be hashed. That is the whole reason this mechanism can never be a FIRST factor.
mfaSection.lastCodeNote: . The step it was in is stored with the enrolment, so that code cannot be used again (RFC 6238 section 5.2).
mfaSection.clearTotpTitle: Clears the enrolment so this person can set up a new one. This is the ONLY way back for somebody who has lost their phone: the secret is on that device and this service cannot reach it.
mfaSection.clearTotpNote: This is the only way back for somebody who has lost their phone. The shared secret lives on that device and this service cannot reach it, and there is deliberately no self-service reset — a second factor anybody can remove is not a second factor. Clearing drops the account to one factor and cannot lock anybody out, because a one-time code is never a way in by itself. They set a new one up at /portal/mfa.
mfaSection.primaryTitle: Signs them in on its own — this is a way IN rather than a second factor.
mfaSection.removePrimaryTitle: This may be the only credential on the account. The removal is REFUSED if it would leave nobody able to sign in.
mfaSection.removeTitle: Removes this passkey. The account drops to one factor and stays reachable.
mfaSection.signCountNote: The sign count is WebAuthn's replay defence: an authenticator's counter only ever goes up, so one that went backwards is a cloned key and the assertion is refused. A counter stuck at zero is an authenticator that does not implement one, which is allowed and is what most platform authenticators do — and every synced passkey.
mfaSection.keysSelf: They create one themselves at /portal/keys, at the sign-in screen, or while spending an activation link. There is no way to create one from here and there cannot be: a WebAuthn ceremony happens in the person's own browser against their own authenticator, and this console is not that browser.
mfaSection.keysOffBefore: Passkeys are switched off in this realm (webauthn.enabled on
mfaSection.keysOffAfter: ), so nobody new can create one. A passkey already registered goes on working.
mfaSection.keysNeedWrite: Renaming or removing a passkey needs Admin Write.
mfaSection.realmAllows: What this realm currently allows: a key may be a primary credential — {primary, select, yes {yes} other {NO}} — and a second factor — {mfa, select, yes {yes} other {NO}} — with at most {max} per person. Those refuse an ENROLMENT and never an authentication, so a key above in a role this realm no longer allows goes on working.
mfaSection.recoveryAuto: A set is created automatically the first time this person enrols a second factor — a confirmed authenticator app, or a security key in the mfa role. There is no control anywhere that issues one on request, here or on /portal or on /admin-api: a way back that somebody has to remember to ask for produces exactly the population it exists to protect, one person at a time. Nobody with a second factor enrolled BEFORE 2026-09-10 has a set, which is the ordinary reason this says none — clearing and re-enrolling is what issues one.
mfaSection.recoveryOffBefore: Recovery codes are switched off in this realm (the authentication policy on
mfaSection.recoveryOffAfter: ), so no new set will be issued. A set already issued goes on working.
mfaSection.recoveryUnreadable: A set exists and this process cannot read it — {why}. Almost always a set sealed under a key-encryption key that has since been rotated. They are REFUSED at the recovery screen rather than let through, and the codes cannot be shown to them either, so this set is worth nothing until it is cleared — after which the next second factor they enrol issues a new one.
mfaSection.allUsed: of {total} — every code has been used, so this account has a second factor and no way back. A set is issued once and is never topped up; clearing it below is what lets the next enrolment issue a new one.
mfaSection.nearlyOut: of {total} — nearly out, and they are not topped up.
mfaSection.issuedOnce: . Once. Enrolling a different second factor does not reissue them, deliberately: somebody who printed a list and later replaced their authenticator app would otherwise be holding strings that had stopped working with nothing having said so.
mfaSection.encryptedBefore: — AES-256-GCM under this service's key-encryption key, so
mfaSection.asShown: as the strings they were shown — development mode, where the key-encryption key is generated per run and encrypting them would mean a printed recovery list that stopped working at the next restart, which is the precise failure this mechanism exists to prevent.
mfaSection.notHashed: ENCRYPTED AND NOT HASHED, unlike userPassword, and for a product reason rather than an arithmetic one: the person may look at their remaining codes again on /portal/mfa, and a hash cannot be shown.
mfaSection.neverShown: This console never shows the codes themselves, and there is no control here or on /admin-api that does. They are a working second factor; showing them to whoever holds Admin Read would be the same door this page already refuses to open for an authenticator enrolment. The person reads them back on their own /portal/mfa.
mfaSection.clearCodesTitle: Deletes the set. This is the ONLY way to a second set: the next second factor this person enrols issues a new one. It cannot lock anybody out — a recovery code is never a way in by itself — but it does take away their way back.
mfaSection.clearCodesNote: Clearing is the only route to a second set. It cannot lock anybody out — a recovery code is never a way in on its own — but it removes the way BACK, so a person whose set is cleared and who then loses their phone needs you again. The sequence that issues a new set is: clear this, have them clear and re-enrol their second factor, and the enrolment issues one.

userCredentialsSection.heading: Credentials: assertion key pairs
userCredentialsSection.lead: What this person can SIGN an authorization grant with: a key pair for RFC 7523’s JWT bearer assertion and one for RFC 7522’s SAML 2.0 bearer assertion, on their own directory entry. A person’s assertion may only be about themselves — the token endpoint refuses one naming anybody else as its sub or <Subject>, because a key on one person’s entry is that person’s credential rather than permission to speak for others. A party that may assert about other people is an APPLICATION with the issuer declared on it. The two profiles’ key pairs share no attribute, so neither signs for the other and taking one off leaves the other working.
userCredentialsSection.noDirectory: This process has no directory, so nobody can hold an assertion key pair.
userCredentialsSection.noEntry: {key} has no entry under ou=users in this realm, so there is nowhere to put a key pair. An identity this service has seen without a directory entry — a client, a bind DN, a subject somebody else asserted — cannot hold one.
userCredentialsSection.shownOnce: It was shown once, when it was issued, and nothing opens it again — not this page, not /admin-api. Issuing again replaces it.
userCredentialsSection.theyKeep: The person keeps their own private key.
userCredentialsSection.noneHeld: No key pair is held for this profile. Issue one from this realm’s certificate authority, or upload a certificate the person already holds.
userCredentialsSection.declaredBefore: An issuer is declared for it (
userCredentialsSection.declaredAfter: ) and nothing can be signed under it until a key pair is here.
userCredentialsSection.needsWrite: Replacing or taking off a key pair needs Admin Write.

userCredentialsSection.issue: Issue a key pair from this realm’s CA
userCredentialsSection.noCaBefore: This realm has no certificate authority yet, so there is nothing to issue a key pair from.
userCredentialsSection.buildOne: Build one on the PKI page
userCredentialsSection.certTip: The certificate whose key this person's assertions are verified with, in PEM. The certificate only: its private key stays with them.
userCredentialsSection.chainTip: The certificates that issued it, in PEM: every intermediate and the root.
userCredentialsSection.chainPem: Chain (PEM, every intermediate and the root)
userCredentialsSection.chainAreaTip: Every intermediate and the root, in PEM.
userCredentialsSection.uploadTip: Put this certificate on their entry for this profile, replacing the key pair held for it.
userCredentialsSection.takeOffTip: Take the key pair off this entry. Not revocation: the certificate stays valid and this service stops accepting what it signs.
userCredentialsSection.notRevocation: Not revocation: the certificate stays valid and this service stops accepting what it signs. The declared issuer goes with it; the other profile’s key pair is untouched.
userCredentialsSection.replaceNote: Either way REPLACES the key pair on this entry. Issuing generates a new key pair here and signs it with this realm’s Issuing CA; the private key is sealed on the entry and shown once, on the page the button opens. Uploading registers a certificate the person already holds, and this service keeps no private key for it. A certificate from THIS realm’s authority may be uploaded alone, and must have been issued to this person. One from any other authority must come with its full chain — every intermediate and the self-signed root — and every link is verified. An upload carrying a private key is refused.
userCredentialsSection.selfService: The person can also issue themselves an RFC 7523 key pair at /portal/signing-key; that door offers the JWT profile only.
federationLinks.heading: Federation links
federationLinks.lead: A link says that ONE partner's identifier for somebody — OpenID Connect's iss and sub, a SAML persistent NameID and the partner's entity ID — is this person. A partner signs in only the person its subject is linked to; a relationship under link-at-first-sign-in makes the link itself after the person signs in here. Removing a link ends every session that partner signed them in to, and their next sign-in through it is treated as unlinked.
federationLinks.noSuch: (no such service-provider-side relationship here — this link matches nothing)
federationLinks.none: No partner's subject is linked to this person.
federationLinks.needsWrite: Adding or removing a link needs Admin Write.
federationLinks.subjectTip: The partner's own identifier for this person: the ID Token's sub, or the persistent NameID. Not their name or address.
federationLinks.noRelationship: There is no service-provider-side relationship in this realm to link through.
userGnapGrantsSection.heading: GNAP grants
userGnapGrantsSection.lead: Every GNAP (RFC 9635) grant this person is the resource owner of: approved by them on the approval page, or acted on by a trusted client presenting a verified assertion about them. Revoke is the client's own section 5.4 act performed for them: every token issued under the grant stops working, the grant is finalized as revoked and CAEP session-revoked is sent. The person can do the same on their own /portal/gnap.
userGnapGrantsSection.none: This person is the resource owner of no GNAP grant in this realm.
userKerberosSection.noKdc: Trust realm {realm} has no KDC ({reason}), so there is no Kerberos principal for this person and no keytab to make.
userKerberosSection.noEntry: This identity has no entry in this realm's directory, which is the one its KDC reads, so it is not a Kerberos principal here.
userKerberosSection.productKdc: product — keyed from their own password
userKerberosSection.developmentKdc: development — every user is keyed from krb5.userPassword, not from their own password

userKerberosSection.refusedUntil: , so the KDC refuses them until their next verified sign-in
userKerberosSection.getThem: — they get them the first time a password is set or verified here
userKerberosSection.why: A keytab is as good as their password: whoever holds it gets a Kerberos ticket as them (kinit -k -t). This service never reads a stored key back out, so a keytab is DERIVED from a password in hand — and the only password you can have in hand for somebody else is one you set now. The person can make their own, from their own password, on /portal/kerberos.
userKerberosSection.needsWrite: Resetting the password for a keytab needs Admin Write.
userKerberosSection.enableFirst: The account is disabled, so a keytab for it could not sign in. Enable it first.
userKerberosSection.resetWarn: This CHANGES {key}'s password: their old one stops working for every protocol, the Kerberos kvno moves up by one, and they are signed out of everything. They are NOT asked to change it at their next sign-in, because that would end the keytab. With a generated password nobody is shown it, and the keytab is the only thing that signs them in until a password is set again.
userKerberosSection.passwordTip: The new password; their Kerberos keys and the keytab are derived from it.
userKerberosSection.randomTip: Generate a password nobody is shown instead of the one typed; only the keytab then signs them in.
userKerberosSection.random: or a generated one that is never shown
userKerberosSection.resetTitle: Sets the password, signs them out everywhere, and shows the keytab derived from it once.

personFieldsSection.noEntry: There is no directory entry for this person here, so there is nothing to change. The Directory entry tab says why.

personFieldsSection.saveTip: Write this tab to the person's entry. Nothing on the other tabs changes, and a refused value is shown with what was typed kept.
personFieldsSection.lead: One tab per group, each with its own Save, writing {dn} in place as an ldapmodify would — and the directory tells Shared Signals of the change as it tells it of a SCIM or LDAP write. Save writes what changed on that tab and nothing else: a single value is set, and an empty one is cleared; a list has the values put in added and the values taken out removed. A list shows one box per value, with + to add one and the bin to delete one; every box that is there must hold a value. A tab of six fields or more opens on its simplified view, the attributes usually filled in; its advanced view shows every one, and an attribute the simplified view hides keeps its value when the tab is saved. An identity verification covers a value only while the entry still holds it, so changing a verified value lets that verification lapse for it.

userAttributesSection.noEntry: There is no directory entry for this person here, so there is nothing to change. The section above says why.
userAttributesSection.listingSummary: What each attribute takes, and what is not offered
userAttributesSection.explain: These write {dn} in place, one attribute at a time, as an ldapmodify of it would — and the directory tells Shared Signals of the change as it tells it of a SCIM or LDAP write. Set replaces every value with one (empty clears it); Add to and Remove from act on one value of an attribute that holds several. An identity verification covers a value only while the entry still holds it, so changing a verified value lets that verification lapse for it.
userAttributesSection.willNotBefore: What these will not change. The password and every other credential (the Credentials tab), the address (its own form on the Attributes tab, because a write of it is verified), the username and the attribute the entry is named by, binary values such as certificates and photographs, group memberships (
userAttributesSection.willNotAfter: ), and what this service records about their sign-ins. ldapmodify still reaches those; the difference between offering an operation and merely not preventing it is the point.
controls.heading: Password and second-factor controls
controls.noStore: No credential store is installed in this process, so there is nothing here to reset.
controls.mustChange: — must be changed at their next sign-in
controls.holdNone: ; they hold none, so their next sign-in asks them to enrol one
controls.signals: Every control below says what it did over Shared Signals: a CAEP credential-change for each credential set, revoked or removed; RISC account-credential-change-required for a reset or a reset link; RISC recovery-information-changed when recovery codes go. Each goes to every stream that asked for the type and covers this person, subject to caep.autoEmitTypes, risc.autoEmitTypes and the RISC opt-out state.
controls.needsWrite: Resetting a password, disabling a credential or requiring a second factor needs Admin Write.
controls.compromisedTip: Tick when the password is known or suspected to be compromised: the RISC event sent is credential-compromise instead of an ordinary credential change.
controls.resetNote: Reset password sets a generated password and shows it to you ONCE — note it and give it to them. They must choose their own at their next sign-in, and they are signed out of everything now. Generate a reset link instead REMOVES the password they have, signs them out of everything, and shows you a single-use link to send them, valid for security.passwordResetTtlMinutes; at it they choose a new password under this realm's password policy.
controls.compromisedNote: Tick the password was compromised when that is WHY you are resetting it: RISC receivers are then also told credential-compromise. A reset link always tells them recovery-activated.
controls.resetTitle: A generated password, shown once; they change it at next sign-in; they are signed out everywhere.
controls.issueLinkTitle: Removes their current password, signs them out everywhere, and shows a single-use link to send them — or mails it to them.
controls.disableKeysNote: Removes all {count} primary security key(s), so a passkey no longer signs them in without a password. A key they hold as a second factor is untouched.
controls.noPassword: They have no password, so their primary keys are the only way they can sign in and disabling them is refused. Reset the password or issue a reset link first.
controls.noKeys: They hold no primary security key, so there is no passwordless sign-in to disable.
controls.disableMfaNote: Disable all MFA removes their authenticator app, every security key in the mfa role and their recovery codes. It cannot lock them out — none of those is a way in. {required, select, yes {A second factor is still required of them, so their next sign-in asks them to enrol a new one.} other {A password alone signs them in afterwards.}}
controls.disableMfaTitle: Removes the authenticator app, mfa keys and recovery codes.
controls.noSecond: They hold no second factor, so there is nothing to disable.
controls.requiredOfThem: A second factor is required of them on their account.
controls.stopRequiring: Stop requiring MFA for this person
controls.stopRequiringTitle: Takes the per-account requirement off; a realm requirement is unaffected.
controls.requireNote: Require MFA makes the sign-in screen ask them for a second factor — and, while they hold none, to enrol an authenticator app or a security key before it signs them in. A passwordless sign-in is refused while it is required.
controls.realmRequires: The realm already requires it of everybody (the
controls.requireMfaTitle: They must use a second factor, and enrol one at their next sign-in if they hold none.
controls.enableNote: The account is disabled. Enabling it lets them sign in again; nothing ended by the disable comes back, and RISC receivers are told account-enabled.
controls.enableTitle: Clears pwdAccountLockedTime; they sign in afresh.
controls.disableNote: Disable the account refuses them at every door — every sign-in, every token grant (a refresh token included), a Kerberos AS-REQ, an LDAP bind, this console and the management API — and ends everything they hold now, as a global logout does: back-channel Logout Tokens go to their relying parties, CAEP session-revoked and RISC account-disabled to the receivers. Front-channel notifications need their own browser and are not sent from here. SCIM active: false is the same act.
controls.disableTitle: Sets pwdAccountLockedTime and signs them out of everything.
controls.reasonTip: The reason the RISC account-disabled event gives its receivers, if any.
controls.hijacking: hijacking — the account was taken over
controls.bulk: bulk-account — one of many created in bulk
controls.delegationBefore: stsNotDelegated is Kerberos's NOT_DELEGATED for WS-Trust OnBehalfOf / ActAs and the RFC 8693 token exchange: while it is set nobody may act for them, whatever any application's delegation attributes say (enforced in product mode; see
controls.delegationAfter: ). It is {set, select, yes {set} other {not set}}. stsMayAct names the one party who may act for them — their access tokens carry it as may_act — and is {has, select, yes {{mayAct}} other {empty}}.
controls.setMayAct: Set who may act for them
controls.delegateTip: The DN of the one person or application that may act for them, carried in their access tokens as may_act. Empty clears it.
controls.setSemanticsTitle: Writes stsDelegationSemantics and stsDefaultDelegationSemantics. Nothing ticked leaves it to the policy: both are allowed for a subject, delegation only for an actor.
controls.delegationTip: Allow delegation: the actor acts for them and is named in the token as act.
controls.impersonationTip: Allow impersonation: the actor is issued a token as them, with no act naming the actor.
controls.defaultTip: The semantics used when a request does not say which it wants.
controls.noDefault: none — the request or the realm decides
